items.title: Leica Revives Its Rare Hammertone Finish for the M-A and M11-P Cameras
items.summary:
Summary 

Leica releases the M-A and M11-P cameras featuring a rare, vintage hammertone finish.The analog and digital models pair textured solid brass with vulcanite-style leatherette.Available worldwide, the premium cameras retail for approx. $7,100 - $10,100 USD, respectively.

Leica is reviving one of the rarest finishes in its archive with the M-A Hammertone and M11-P Hammertone, two special-edition rangefinders that wrap their top and base plates in a textured, mottled coating. The finish dates back to the 1930s and became shorthand in German industrial design for toughness and dependability, with its signature pattern forming as the coating dries and metallic pigments and additives create slight shifts in surface tension.

On Leica bodies it has appeared only sporadically, from the Leica MD documentation camera built for the Leitz Reprovit system to a 1964 Leica MD produced in a run of just ten, followed by later releases such as the 2003 MP LHSA, the 2011 M9 Hammertone and the 2016 M-A Vienna Edition. For this pair, Leica reworked the process, relying on specialists at its Wetzlar Manufacture to achieve an even result across the texture, and since the surface never forms the same way twice, each camera ends up one of a kind. The solid brass bodies combine that finish with cross-knurled controls, a polished silver shutter-release plate and black vulcanite-style leatherette with white engravings, while the M11-P Hammertone adds softer, rounded edges on its top and base plates and a silver-chrome front screw.

Beneath the vintage-industrial look, both cameras mirror…

items.title: John Goldberger’s ‘100 Superlative Rolex Watches’ Returns in a Fully Revised Edition
items.summary:
Summary 

John Goldberger’s 100 Superlative Rolex Watches returns in a fully revised edition.New photography and updated research spotlight 100 of the rarest Rolex references.Physical copies will hit European stores in December, followed by the rest of the world in Spring 2027.

Nearly two decades after its original 2008 debut helped establish the modern blueprint for vintage Rolex scholarship, Damiani Books is releasing a completely revised edition of John Goldberger ’s landmark reference volume, 100 Superlative Rolex Watches .

Featuring an introduction by Giampiero Negretti, the updated 280-page edition brings together 100 of the rarest and most historically significant Rolex timepieces ever produced, spanning early Oyster models, cloisonné enamel dials, and military-issue Submariners to complicated moonphases and Paul Newman Cosmograph Daytonas. Developed in collaboration with some of the world's foremost collectors, the volume pairs newly commissioned high-resolution photography with updated archival research and previously unseen historical material, examining why vintage Rolex continues to serve as the benchmark at the intersection of luxury, design, and collectibility.

Printed in Italy , the new edition runs to 280 pages and comes as an eco-leather hardcover with a slipcase, measuring 24.2 by 28.5 cm. It's available to order from Damiani Books, retailing at €240 EUR (approx. $265 USD). Physical copies will officially arrive in European bookstores starting December 1, 2026, followed by a wider release across the US and worldwide in Spring 2027.

items.title: Mercedes-Benz Unveils Holographic Tech to Turn Windshields Into Screens
items.summary:
Summary 

Mercedes-Benz has announced Holo Display technology that turns a vehicle windshield into a transparent screenUsing a dashboard projector and laminated holographic film the system displays sunlight-readable visuals tailored separately to driver and passenger viewing anglesThe automaker is also developing Intelligent Display in Glass to project safety symbols and traffic warnings through side and rear windows

German luxury automaker Mercedes-Benz has announced its new Holo Display and Intelligent Display in Glass technologies, expanding automotive screens directly onto vehicle windows. Building upon the dashboard-spanning Hyperscreen introduced earlier this decade, both next-generation display systems remain virtually invisible to the naked eye when not actively in use.

Currently termed the Holo Display, the windshield system pairs a dashboard-integrated projector with a specialized transparent film laminated onto the interior glass. Utilizing holographic optical elements to reflect light wavelengths emitted by the projector, the setup produces imagery strong enough to remain legible even in bright sunlight, improving upon current-generation head-up displays. Engineered to prevent distraction, the display restricts viewing angles so drivers and passengers see isolated visuals—delivering navigation and vehicle data to the driver while offering passengers video calls, journey points of interest, and films.

Alongside the windshield projection setup, Mercedes-Benz is developing Intelligent Display in Glass for a vehicle's side and rear windows. Integrating subtle…

items.title: Alessio Ascari on What Lasts Once the Hype Dies Down

As the founder of KALEIDOSCOPE and Capsule, Alessio Ascari is one of the few figures in design publishing who translates ideas into physical spaces—from Spazio Maiocchi in Milan and Manifesto in Paris to the annual roaming event Capsule Plaza. This month, Capsule Plaza touches down in Shanghai for the first time, taking over IYOUTH STUDIO from November 10 to 15. Taking advantage of the occasion, Hypebeast sat down with Alessio for an exclusive conversation, spanning his recent observations of Shanghai's design scene, the changing relationship between younger generations and design, and his take on the true motives behind the industry's "crossover" frenzy—ultimately asking: when the hype fades, what is worth holding onto?

The Shanghai Design Landscape You’ve visited Shanghai frequently recently to prepare for this Capsule Plaza. What excites you most about the current design ecosystem here? Specifically, what shifts are happening that the outside world might not fully realize yet? 

I really love the energy of Shanghai. What excites me most is the collision between tradition and innovation: cultural heritage and craftsmanship on one side, technological advancement and forward-thinking on the other. There’s also a subcultural and experimental side to Shanghai’s creative scene that outsiders might not be familiar with, but it’s incredibly cool and dynamic. Youth culture is strong here, and people have an international, open mindset, which fills the city with possibilities.

items.title: Jamie Pearl on the Art of Photographing Fame
items.summary:
Summary 

Jamie Pearl reflects on capturing candid moments with Doechii, Dennis Rodman, Nina Dobrev and other cultural figures.From spontaneous celebrity portraits to experimental editorial work, the photographer shares a creative approach shaped by energy, instinct and authenticity.

Some of the most memorable celebrity photographs happen when no one's quite ready for the camera. A cigarette break outside a Fashion Week dinner, a fleeting moment in the backseat of a car, or the final touches before a red carpet appearance can reveal more personality than a carefully staged portrait. For New York-based photographer Jamie Pearl , those in-between moments have become the foundation of a practice rooted in spontaneity and human connection.

After discovering black-and-white film photography in high school, Jamie eventually found a footing in New York's fashion and entertainment circles, capturing everyone from Dennis Rodman and Doechii to Keke Palmer and Nina Dobrev. While the fast-paced world of celebrity events has sharpened an instinct for the unexpected, a growing interest in editorial photography has opened up new possibilities for creative experimentation. 

We caught up with Jamie to discuss memorable encounters, the art of thinking on your feet, and why the best images often happen when you least expect them.

"In the words of one of my favorite photographers, Tyrell Hampton, it’s all about energy."

items.title: Barry McGee Is Back for ‘Another Round’ with Jeffrey Deitch
items.summary:
Summary 

Artist Barry McGee has unveiled a new "solo" exhibition at Jeffrey Deitch's Los Angeles outpost, titled 'Another Round'The exhibition, running through January 30, 2027, features over 200 paintings, sculptures, and photographs by McGee alongside hundreds of works from friends and collaborators, including a mini fabrication of '99CENTS,' his knockout anti-art fair presentation earlier this year

After he opened a knockout 99CENT in February, artist Barry McGee is back in Los Angeles for Another Round , his new exhibition at Jeffrey Deitch 's Santa Monica Boulevard space. The graffiti writer-turned contemporary art star gathers over 200 paintings, sculptures, and photographs to envelope the space. It's his first show with Deitch in 20 years, and in the spirit of the Frieze anti-fair, was made possible with a little help from his friends.

While billed as such, the show is less of a “solo” than a snapshot of McGee's place in the art world: his curatorial style and unique place in high-low culture. “In this day and age, a solo anything seems ridiculous,” he recently told The Los Angeles Times. “The ego of the artist is a tricky thing.”

Highlights include a bulbous hang of prints and photographs oozing from the walls of the main gallery and kaleidoscopic tiled works peppered throughout. Crowded between them are works by the likes of CHITO , Chris Lux, Todd James , Tom Franco, C. R. Stecky III, and more, like a painted bench by Alfonzo Gonzalez Jr. and KATSU 's incognito tagger, a robotic arm spraying from the inside of a bush.

Another Round also includes two mock…

items.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
items.summary:
All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe

I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that.

Which is what happened at Prada this season. The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. There were stiff boxy pleated skirts and tube skirts painted with swirls, and dainty embellished skirts with a layer of gauze on top, like a petticoat worn on the outside.
